7520:
Haste means doing something very quickly because you feel a strong urge or pressure to get it done fast. But it is not just any kind of speed. Haste is speed that is driven by urgency — a feeling that you must move fast, that there is no time to slow down.

Think of the difference between a runner who carefully trains and runs a race at full speed, versus a person who overslept and is frantically throwing their belongings into a bag to catch a bus. The runner is fast. The person with the bag is acting in haste.
What Makes Haste Different from Just "Speed" or "Quickness"

This is the most important thing to understand. Haste is not a neutral word. It carries extra meaning that plain words like "speed" or "quickness" do not.

Haste always implies urgency. You are not moving fast because you feel like it. You are moving fast because something is pushing you — a deadline, a fear, an emergency, a worry.

Haste often implies carelessness. Because you are rushing so much, you may not be thinking clearly or acting carefully. Mistakes happen. Things get forgotten. This is why there is a famous English saying: "Haste makes waste" — meaning that when you rush too much, you end up making mistakes that cost you more time and effort in the end than if you had just slowed down from the beginning.

So haste sits in a unique space: it is speed coloured by urgency and often tinged with a lack of care.

When you use the word haste, you are painting a picture of someone who is:

  • Rushed — not taking the time they normally would
  • Pressured — feeling that time is running out or that something demands immediate action
  • Possibly flustered or careless — skipping steps, not thinking things through fully

It is a word that often carries a slightly negative or cautionary tone, precisely because haste is associated with the risk of things going wrong.

Here are the most natural and common ways you will encounter haste as a noun:

"In haste" — This is the most common phrase. It means something was done quickly and hurriedly, without enough time or care.

  • "She wrote the letter in haste and forgot to sign it."
  • "He left the house in haste and left his keys behind."

"With haste" — Similar to "in haste," but slightly more formal. It emphasizes the quickness of the action.

  • "The soldier returned to camp with haste."

"Make haste" — This is a somewhat old-fashioned or literary phrase meaning "hurry up."

  • "Make haste! The train leaves in five minutes."

"Undue haste" / "great haste" — You will often see haste paired with adjectives that describe how much rushing is happening.

  • "The decision was made with undue haste" means the decision was made more quickly than it should have been — carelessly fast.
  • "They worked with great haste" means they worked extremely fast, driven by urgency.

Haste is not always a small thing. It can describe anything from:

  • A person frantically packing a bag before a flight (small, personal haste)
  • A government rushing a law through parliament without proper discussion (large-scale haste with serious consequences)
  • A surgeon rushing through a procedure (dangerous haste)

In every case, the common thread is the same: speed driven by urgency, often at the cost of careful thinking or proper care.
When Haste Is Justified vs. When It Is Not

This is a useful distinction to understand the word fully.

Sometimes haste is completely understandable and necessary — if there is a fire, you run. If someone is injured, you rush them to hospital. This is haste in response to a genuine emergency, and no one would criticize it.

But very often when people use the word haste — especially in formal writing or serious discussion — they are pointing out that someone moved too fast when they didn't need to, or should not have. The haste was the problem. It led to poor decisions, overlooked details, or avoidable mistakes.

This is why haste often appears in critical or cautionary contexts: "The project failed because of the haste with which it was launched."
Haste is a rapid, urgency-driven quickness in action that often comes at the cost of care, thought, or quality.
7521: Hasten means to make something happen faster, or to move/act quickly yourself. Think of it as adding speed — either to your own actions, or to a process or event in the world.
The two main ways it is used

1. You hasten — meaning you hurry or move quickly

Here, you are the one moving fast. You rush somewhere or do something without delay.

  • She hastened to the hospital when she heard the news.

(= She hurried to the hospital.)

  • He hastened out of the room before anyone could ask him questions.

(= He quickly left the room.)

  • They hastened to finish the project before the deadline.

(= They worked quickly to finish it.)

Notice that in this use, hasten is almost always followed by "to + verb" or a direction (to the door, out of the room, away, back, etc.). You hasten to do something, or toward somewhere.

2. You hasten something — meaning you cause something to happen sooner or faster

Here, you are not the one moving fast. Instead, you are speeding up something else — an event, a process, or an outcome that would have happened eventually, but now happens earlier or quicker because of your action.

  • Stress can hasten the development of heart disease.

(= Stress can make heart disease develop sooner than it otherwise would.)

  • The harsh winter hastened the death of the crops.

(= The winter caused the crops to die faster.)

  • His reckless spending hastened the collapse of the company.

(= It caused the company to collapse sooner than it would have otherwise.)

  • The new medicine hastened her recovery.

(= It made her recovery happen faster.)

This is perhaps the more powerful and commonly tested use of the word. The key idea is that something was already going to happen — hasten just pulls it forward in time, or speeds up its pace.
A very common fixed phrase: "I hasten to add / say / point out"

You will very frequently see hasten used in this expression. It means "I want to quickly say this before you get the wrong idea." The speaker feels a sense of urgency to clarify or correct something immediately.

  • The new policy will reduce costs — I hasten to add, without any reduction in quality.

(= I want to quickly clarify: quality will not suffer.)

  • He is a difficult person to work with, I hasten to say, though extremely talented.

(= I want to quickly point out that he is also talented, so you don't just think he's difficult.)

Think of it as the speaker mentally raising their hand and saying "wait, wait — let me also say this right now before you misunderstand me."
The tone and register of the word

Hasten is a formal word. You would rarely hear it in casual conversation. In everyday speech, people say hurry, rush, speed up, or get a move on. Hasten belongs more to writing — news articles, literature, formal speeches, academic texts, and serious discussions.

Using "hasten" instead of "hurry" gives your sentence a more composed, serious, and polished feel. It doesn't sound panicked or rushed the way "rush" can. It implies purposeful, deliberate speed.

Compare:

  • He rushed to explain himself. → feels urgent, slightly frantic
  • He hastened to explain himself. → feels urgent, but more controlled and dignified
How hasten compares to similar words

Understanding these distinctions will sharpen your sense of the word.

Hurry is the most common everyday substitute. It can mean hasten in both senses, but it's informal and casual. You'd say "hurry up" to a friend, not "hasten."

Rush implies even greater speed, often with a suggestion of carelessness or lack of control. Rushing can lead to mistakes. Hastening generally doesn't carry that risk.

Accelerate means to increase speed, but it is used more for things with mechanical or measurable speed — a car accelerates, a process accelerates. It doesn't quite work for a person walking quickly somewhere.

Expedite means to make a process happen faster, usually in an official or bureaucratic context. You expedite a visa application or a shipment. You wouldn't use expedite for something like someone's death or a natural event.

Hasten is unique because it works elegantly for both human movement and the speeding up of events, and it carries a formal, literary weight that none of the above fully match.

When used in the second sense (causing something to happen sooner), hasten most naturally pairs with events or outcomes that have some natural timeline — things that were going to happen anyway. Common examples in writing:

  • Hasten someone's death, decline, downfall, or departure
  • Hasten the end, collapse, or fall of something
  • Hasten someone's recovery or return
  • Hasten the arrival of something (a change, a new era, etc.)
  • Hasten a process or transition

You would not say "I hastened a sandwich." The word needs something with a natural trajectory — a process, an event, an outcome.
The complete picture in one summary

Hasten means:

  1. To move or act quickly yourself (She hastened away.)
  2. To cause something to happen sooner or faster than it naturally would (The cold hastened his death.)
  3. In the fixed phrase "I hasten to add/say" — to quickly clarify or point out something before a misunderstanding forms.

It is a formal word that implies purposeful, deliberate speed — never panic, never carelessness. It is most at home in writing and serious speech, and it always carries a sense of urgency wrapped in composure.
7522:
Hastily means doing something very quickly, often in a rushed way that leaves little room for care, thought, or proper attention.

When someone does something hastily, two things are usually true at the same time:

  • They are moving or acting fast
  • They are doing it with less care than the situation deserves

These two ideas — speed and carelessness — almost always travel together in this word. That combination is what makes "hastily" special and different from simply meaning "fast."

Think of it this way. Imagine you have a test tomorrow, but you only study for 15 minutes the night before because you forgot about it. You studied hastily. You were rushed, you skipped important parts, and your preparation was sloppy because of the time pressure.

Or imagine someone cooking dinner in 5 minutes by throwing everything together without measuring anything, just to get it done. They cooked hastily.

The key feeling behind "hastily" is: "I need to hurry, even if that means things won't turn out perfectly."

As an adverb, "hastily" describes verbs — it tells you how an action was performed.

  • She hastily packed her bags. (She packed in a rush, probably forgetting things.)
  • He hastily scribbled a note. (He wrote quickly and probably messily.)
  • They hastily made a decision. (They decided without thinking it through properly.)
  • She hastily apologized and left. (Her apology was brief, rushed, maybe not sincere-sounding.)

Notice that in every case, "hastily" sits right before the verb it describes, though it can also appear at the end of a sentence: "She packed her bags hastily."

"Hastily" carries two slightly different flavors depending on context. Both are correct uses of the word.

Shade 1 — Pure speed under pressure
Sometimes "hastily" simply means someone acted very quickly because they had no choice. There's urgency, and they responded to it.

"The soldiers hastily retreated when the enemy advanced."
Here, speed was necessary. There's little judgment about carelessness — the situation just demanded fast action.

Shade 2 — Reckless quickness (the more common shade)
More often, "hastily" carries a mild criticism. It suggests that the person should have taken more time, but didn't — and as a result, something was done poorly, incompletely, or without proper thought.

"The law was hastily written and full of loopholes."
"He hastily judged her without knowing the full story."
"The building was hastily constructed and started falling apart within years."

In these sentences, you can sense that things went wrong because of the rush. This is the most common and important use of "hastily."

"Hastily" almost always carries a negative connotation — meaning it suggests something undesirable. It quietly signals that the quality of an action suffered because of the rush. Even when no one says something went wrong, "hastily" plants that seed of doubt in the reader's or listener's mind.

Compare:

  • "She quickly finished the report." → Neutral. She was efficient.
  • "She hastily finished the report." → Suggests the report may be incomplete or poorly done.

The difference is subtle but real. "Quickly" is about speed alone. "Hastily" is about speed at the cost of something.

Certain words appear with "hastily" very often in natural English. Learning these will help you recognize and use the word naturally.

  • hastily arranged — a hastily arranged meeting (set up at the last minute, possibly disorganized)
  • hastily written — a hastily written email (rushed, possibly with errors or missing information)
  • hastily made — a hastily made decision (not thought through carefully)
  • hastily put together — a hastily put-together plan (lacking proper planning)
  • hastily left / departed — she hastily left the room (she exited in a rush)
  • hastily added — a hastily added note at the bottom (something included at the last moment)
  • hastily concluded — a hastily concluded deal (an agreement reached without enough discussion)

Several words are close in meaning to "hastily," but each one has its own personality.

Quickly / Rapidly / Swiftly — These describe pure speed only. They carry no suggestion of carelessness or poor quality. A surgeon can quickly and perfectly stitch a wound. But you would not say she stitched it hastily if the result was perfect — that would feel wrong.

Hurriedly — This is the closest word to "hastily." They are nearly identical in meaning and can often be swapped. However, "hurriedly" places slightly more emphasis on the state of the person (they were in a hurry, they were flustered), while "hastily" places slightly more emphasis on the quality of the action being rushed. In practice, most native speakers use them interchangeably.

Rashly — This means acting without thinking, but it focuses more on impulsiveness and poor judgment rather than on the speed of the action. You can do something rashly even if you take an hour to do it — as long as you didn't think it through. "Hastily" always involves speed; "rashly" does not necessarily.

Carelessly — This focuses purely on the lack of care, not the speed. You can be careless while taking all the time in the world. "Hastily" always implies speed as the reason for the carelessness.
A Deeper Nuance — Why Something Was Done Hastily

"Hastily" often implies that there was some external pressure that caused the rush — a deadline, a threat, an emergency, or simply poor time management. This is important because it partially explains the person's behavior, even if it doesn't excuse the result.

"The treaty was hastily signed before both sides fully understood its terms."

Here, you understand that something forced both sides to rush. The word creates a sense of "this could have been done better under different circumstances." This gives "hastily" a slightly more forgiving tone than "carelessly" or "sloppily," which suggest fault in the person's character rather than in the circumstances.

Hastily means doing something with excessive speed, in a way that sacrifices care, thought, or proper attention — usually because of time pressure — and often resulting in an outcome that is incomplete, flawed, or regrettable.
7523:
Hasty means doing something too quickly, without enough thought, care, or preparation — and because of that speed, something important gets sacrificed: quality, accuracy, safety, or good judgment.

The key idea is not just speed. It is inappropriate speed — moving faster than the situation deserves or allows.

She made a hasty decision and regretted it later.
He packed his bags in a hasty manner and forgot half his things.
What "Hasty" Really Implies

When you call something hasty, you are making a quiet criticism. You are saying:

  • More time should have been taken.
  • Important steps were skipped.
  • The outcome suffered because of the rush.

This is why "hasty" almost always carries a negative tone. It signals that the speed was a mistake — not a virtue.

Think of it this way: a surgeon who operates quickly is skilled. A surgeon who operates hastily is dangerous. The speed itself is not the problem — the carelessness that comes with the speed is the problem.
"Hasty" vs. "Quick" or "Fast" — A Critical Difference

This is the most important distinction to understand:

  • Quick / Fast → neutral words. They simply describe speed. No judgment attached.
  • Hasty → a judgmental word. It says the speed was excessive and unwise for the situation.
NeutralJudgmental (Hasty)
She gave a quick answer.She gave a hasty answer. (She should have thought more.)
He left fast.He left in a hasty manner. (He left before he should have.)

Actually, let me re-do that without a table:

  • "She gave a quick answer" — neutral. She answered fast. Fine.
  • "She gave a hasty answer" — critical. She answered without thinking properly. Not fine.

The word hasty always whispers: "You should have slowed down."
How and Where "Hasty" Is Used

Hasty can describe both actions and people.

1. Describing Actions or Things

This is the most common use. The action was done with too much rush and too little care.

  • A hasty decision — a choice made without proper thought; often leads to regret.
  • A hasty conclusion — a judgment reached too quickly, before gathering enough information. ("Don't jump to hasty conclusions.")
  • A hasty exit / retreat — leaving a place very quickly, often abruptly or awkwardly.
  • A hasty glance — a very quick, careless look; you didn't really observe properly.
  • Hasty words — things said in the heat of the moment, without thinking; words you might later regret.
  • A hasty meal — food eaten very quickly, without care or enjoyment.
  • A hasty plan — a plan made without enough preparation; likely to have holes in it.

2. Describing a Person

When used to describe a person, hasty means someone who consistently acts impulsively — they rush into things, react before thinking, and often make avoidable mistakes because they don't pause to reflect.

"Don't be so hasty — think before you speak."
"He is a hasty person; he never waits to hear the full story before reacting."
The Idea of "Jumping Ahead"

A very natural way to picture hasty is the idea of jumping steps.

Imagine building a house. There is a proper sequence: design → foundation → walls → roof. A hasty builder skips steps — maybe pours the foundation before the design is ready, or builds walls before the foundation is solid. The result? A weak, flawed house.

Hasty always involves this kind of skipping — of thought, of time, of care — that the situation truly needed.
Degrees of Hastiness

Hasty can range from mildly careless to seriously reckless, depending on the context:

  • Mildly hasty: You wrote an email quickly and forgot to attach the file.
  • Moderately hasty: You made a hasty financial decision and lost some money.
  • Seriously hasty: A leader made a hasty judgment in a crisis and caused harm.

The word itself doesn't change — but the weight of it depends on the stakes of the situation.
When "Hasty" Is Slightly Less Negative

In rare cases, hasty can describe urgency-driven speed without heavy criticism — especially when the context makes the rush understandable.

"They made a hasty escape from the burning building."

Here, the speed was necessary. The word still signals that things were rushed and not orderly, but it doesn't strongly blame anyone. However, even in these cases, the word still carries the flavor of rushed and less-than-ideal.
Synonyms (Words Close in Meaning)

• Rash — very similar; emphasizes acting without thinking, often with dangerous results.
  • Impulsive — acting on sudden feelings without reflection.
  • Rushed — done in a hurry; close in meaning but slightly more neutral than hasty.
  • Reckless — stronger; shows complete disregard for consequences.
  • Hurried — moving quickly due to time pressure; less judgmental than hasty.
  • Precipitate (formal) — acting too soon, before things are ready.

Among these, rash and hasty are the closest pair. The small difference: rash often emphasizes the risk or danger of acting without thought, while hasty emphasizes the speed that caused the lack of thought.
Antonyms (Opposite Meanings)

• Careful — giving proper attention and time.
  • Deliberate — done with full intention and thought; the opposite of accidental or rushed.
  • Considered — thought about properly before acting.
  • Measured — calm, controlled, and proportionate.
  • Cautious — careful to avoid mistakes or danger.
  • Unhurried — relaxed in pace; no undue rush.
A Memorable Way to Remember It

Think of the phrase: "Haste makes waste."
(Rushing causes mistakes, and mistakes waste time, effort, and resources.)

Hasty is simply the adjective born from that same idea. When something is hasty, it is poisoned by haste — by that dangerous, reckless rush that skips the care the moment deserved.
Summary in One Sentence

Hasty means done or decided too quickly and without sufficient thought or care, in a way that typically leads to mistakes, poor results, or regret — and it almost always carries a tone of gentle-to-strong criticism of that speed.
7524:
A hatch is a small opening or doorway — one that is built into a flat surface like a floor, a ceiling, a wall, or the deck of a ship — and that usually has a cover or door that you can open and close over it.

Think of it as a hidden or built-in gateway between two spaces, designed to let a person or things pass through when needed, but which stays closed the rest of the time.

1. An opening in a floor, ceiling, deck, or roof

This is the most common meaning. A hatch is an access point cut into a surface that you normally walk on, stand under, or sit on top of. It connects one level or compartment to another.

  • A ship has hatches on its deck — rectangular openings through which cargo is loaded into the hold below, or through which crew members can climb down.
  • A submarine has hatches on its top — the round doors you see sailors climbing through when a sub is on the surface.
  • Many homes have a loft hatch (also called an attic hatch) — a small opening in the ceiling that you push open to get into the attic space above.
  • Old houses often had a cellar hatch in the floor — a trapdoor-like opening that led down to the storage area below.

In all these cases, the hatch serves the same purpose: it is a built-in opening that allows access to a space that is otherwise closed off.

The word can refer to the opening itself, or to the lid/door that covers it — both uses are correct and common. So "open the hatch" means either opening the cover or passing through the opening. Context makes it clear.

2. A small window-like opening cut into a wall (a serving hatch)

A hatch doesn't always have to be in a floor or ceiling. It can also be a small rectangular opening cut through a wall — usually so that things can be passed through from one room to another without anyone having to walk around.

The most familiar example is a serving hatch: an opening cut through the wall between a kitchen and a dining room, so that a person in the kitchen can pass food directly through the wall to someone in the dining room. Many older homes and traditional restaurants have these.

The key idea here is the same — a hatch is an opening that allows passage (of people or things) without the need to use a full door.
Escape Hatch — a very important phrase

You will often hear the phrase escape hatch. This literally refers to a hatch on an aircraft, spacecraft, submarine, or tank that is specifically designed to be used in emergencies — a way to get out quickly when the normal exit is unavailable or blocked.

In everyday language, "escape hatch" is also used figuratively to mean a way out of a difficult situation — a backup plan, a loophole, or an option that lets you get out of a commitment or a problem. For example: "The vague wording of the contract gave the company an escape hatch."
The Hatch on a Ship — worth understanding fully

Ships deserve a bit more detail here because the word is most strongly associated with maritime use.

On a ship, a hatch (also called a hatchway) is a large opening on the deck (the flat top surface of the ship). It is covered by a hatch cover — a heavy lid or a series of panels that seal it shut. When cargo needs to be loaded or unloaded, the hatch cover is removed and goods are lowered into or lifted out of the cargo hold below.

The phrase "batten down the hatches" comes from seafaring — before a storm, sailors would seal the hatch covers tightly (using wooden strips called battens) so that water couldn't get in. Today, this phrase is used figuratively to mean "prepare for something difficult or dangerous that is coming."

• In aviation and spacecraft: rockets, capsules, and space stations have hatches — the round or oval doors that astronauts use to enter, exit, or move between modules. These are designed to seal airtight.
  • In military vehicles: tanks and armored vehicles have hatches on top through which the crew can poke their heads out or exit the vehicle.
  • In art: a hatch (and especially cross-hatch) refers to one of a series of fine, parallel lines drawn close together to create the effect of shadow or shading in a drawing or engraving. Multiple parallel lines are collectively called hatching, and overlapping lines in two directions are called cross-hatching.
  • A brood: less commonly, "hatch" can also refer to the group of young animals — typically birds or fish — that came from a set of eggs all at once. For example, "The whole hatch of chicks was healthy."
Summary of all meanings at a glance

SenseWhat it is
Opening in a floor/ceiling/deckA built-in access point that can be covered/sealed
The cover/door over that openingThe lid or door itself
Opening in a wallA small pass-through window, like a serving hatch
Escape hatchAn emergency exit; figuratively, a way out of trouble
Art termA fine line in a drawing used for shading
A broodA group of young from the same batch of eggs
One Line to Remember It By

A hatch is a small built-in opening — in a floor, wall, ceiling, or deck — that connects one space to another and can be opened and closed, and by extension, anything resembling or functioning like such an opening.
7525: The word hatch has three distinct meanings as a verb. Each meaning is quite different from the others, so it's important to understand all three clearly.
Meaning 1 — A baby animal breaking out of an egg

This is the most common and well-known meaning. When a baby animal (like a chick, a turtle, a fish, or a snake) grows inside an egg and finally breaks through the shell to come out into the world, we say it hatches.

Think of it this way: The egg is like a tiny sealed room. The baby animal is trapped inside, growing slowly. When it's finally ready, it cracks the shell open and comes out. That moment — and the whole process of it — is called hatching.

Examples:

  • "The eggs will hatch in about three weeks."
  • "Three baby chicks hatched this morning."
  • "The snake hatched from a small white egg."

Important detail — who does the hatching?
You can use this verb in two directions:

  • The baby animal hatches. → "The chick hatched." (The chick did the breaking out.)
  • The egg hatches. → "The egg hatched." (The egg opened up.)
  • The parent hatches the eggs. → "The hen is hatching her eggs." (Here it means the mother bird is sitting on the eggs, keeping them warm, so they will eventually open. She is causing the hatching to happen.)

So depending on your sentence, the subject can be the baby animal, the egg, or the parent — and all three uses are correct.
Meaning 2 — To secretly create a plan

This meaning has nothing to do with eggs or animals. When people hatch a plan, a scheme, or a plot, it means they think it up and develop it — usually in secret, and usually when the plan is clever, sneaky, or cunning.

Think of it this way: Just like a baby chick grows quietly and secretly inside an egg before it finally comes out, a plan can also grow quietly inside someone's mind (or in a secret meeting) before it is finally revealed or carried out. The idea is that the plan was being developed in hiding — and this is exactly why "hatch" is used for both eggs and secret plans. The feeling is the same: something is quietly growing in the dark, and then it comes out.

Examples:

  • "The two friends hatched a plan to sneak out of school."
  • "The villain spent months hatching a scheme to take over the company."
  • "We hatched a plot to surprise her on her birthday."

Key nuances to remember:

  • The word almost always implies secrecy. You don't usually say someone hatched a plan if the plan was completely open and innocent. There's always a sense of "behind closed doors."
  • It is often (but not always) used for plans that are mischievous, cunning, or even dishonest — though it can be used for fun, harmless surprises too.
  • You almost always hatch something — a plan, a scheme, a plot, a conspiracy, an idea. You don't usually use "hatch" alone without an object in this meaning.
Meaning 3 — To draw thin parallel lines (an art technique)

This is a more specialized meaning, mostly used in art and drawing. When an artist hatches a surface, they draw many thin, closely spaced, parallel lines on it. These lines are not meant to spell anything or make a pattern for its own sake — they are used to create the effect of shadow, shade, or depth in a drawing.

Think of it this way: Imagine a black-and-white pencil drawing of a face. The dark areas — the shadows under the nose, the shading on the cheek — aren't colored in with a solid black fill. Instead, the artist draws dozens of tiny lines, packed closely together, to make that area look darker. That technique is called hatching.

Examples:

  • "The artist hatched the shadowy areas of the portrait to make them look darker."
  • "He hatched the background with fine, careful strokes."

A related term — cross-hatching:
When an artist draws one set of parallel lines and then draws another set of lines crossing over them (like a grid or an X pattern), it is called cross-hatching. This creates an even darker, richer shadow effect. You'll often hear both "hatch" and "cross-hatch" used together in art contexts.
Quick Summary of All Three Meanings

• Hatch (eggs/animals): A baby animal breaks out of its egg, or a parent keeps eggs warm so they open. → "The eggs hatched on Sunday."
  • Hatch (a plan): To secretly think up and develop a clever or cunning plan. → "They hatched a scheme to fool everyone."
  • Hatch (in drawing): To draw thin parallel lines to create shading or depth in artwork. → "She hatched the shadows carefully with a fine pencil."

The context of a sentence will almost always make it crystal clear which meaning is intended — because eggs, secret plans, and art shading are very different subjects. Just ask yourself: Is this sentence about animals and eggs? Is it about a secret plan? Is it about drawing? — and the meaning will be obvious every time.
7526: A hatchet is a small, lightweight tool used for chopping. Think of it as a miniature version of an axe — one you can hold and swing comfortably with just one hand.

A hatchet has two main parts:

The head — a solid piece of metal at the top. One side of the head has a sharp blade (the cutting edge), and the opposite side is flat and blunt, almost like a small hammer. That blunt side can actually be used for hammering, which makes the hatchet a two-in-one tool.

The handle — a short grip, usually made of wood or a tough synthetic material, attached to the head. Because the handle is short (roughly the length of your forearm), the whole tool is compact and easy to carry.

A typical hatchet is about 10 to 15 inches long and light enough to hold in one hand without strain.
How it's different from an axe

People often picture an axe when they first hear "hatchet," and they're right to — both are cutting tools with the same basic design. The key difference is size and purpose:

  • An axe is large, heavy, and meant to be swung with both hands. It's for big jobs: felling trees, splitting large logs.
  • A hatchet is small, light, and one-handed. It's built for smaller, quicker jobs.

Think of an axe as a full-sized sledgehammer and a hatchet as a regular hammer. Same idea, very different scale.

A hatchet is essentially a portable chopping tool, most commonly used in:

  • Camping and outdoor survival — chopping branches, making tent stakes, clearing a path
  • Starting a fire — splitting wood into small, thin pieces called kindling (kindling catches fire easily and helps a larger fire get going)
  • Light woodwork — shaping or trimming wood in simple carpentry tasks
  • General cutting — cutting rope, clearing brush, and other rough outdoor tasks

It's a staple of camping gear kits precisely because it's compact, versatile, and effective.

• "He packed a hatchet in his backpack before the hiking trip."
  • "She used the hatchet to split the logs into kindling."
  • "The hatchet's blade was dull after months of use and needed sharpening."

The word "hatchet" appears in a few important English expressions you'll encounter regularly:

1. "Bury the hatchet"
This is a very common idiom meaning to end a conflict and make peace. When two people (or groups) "bury the hatchet," they agree to stop fighting, forgive each other, and move forward.

Example: "The two brothers hadn't spoken in years, but they finally buried the hatchet at their mother's birthday dinner."

The phrase comes from a tradition among some Native American peoples, where rival groups would literally bury their weapons in the ground as a ceremony of peace — a physical act of saying, "We are done fighting."

2. "Hatchet job"
This phrase means a deliberately harsh, unfair, or destructive attack on someone's reputation or work — especially in writing, like a review or a news article. A "hatchet job" isn't honest criticism; it's the kind of vicious, one-sided attack meant to destroy rather than fairly evaluate.

Example: "That journalist wrote a real hatchet job on the new film — it felt less like a review and more like a personal attack on the director."

The image is vivid: instead of carefully examining something, the writer just swings a hatchet at it.

3. "Hatchet man" / "Hatchet person"
This refers to a person whose job is to carry out harsh, unpleasant tasks on behalf of someone more powerful — tasks like firing employees, cutting budgets, or intimidating rivals. The hatchet man does the "dirty work" so that the person in charge doesn't have to.

Example: "The CEO sent his hatchet man to deliver the news of the layoffs."
The overall feel of the word

Physically, a hatchet is a practical, no-nonsense tool — sturdy, direct, uncomplicated. And this character carries into the language too. Phrases built around "hatchet" tend to involve forceful, blunt action: ending things decisively, attacking harshly, doing difficult jobs without hesitation. The word itself carries a kind of sharp, no-frills energy.
7527:
A hatchet job is a piece of writing, a speech, or a broadcast that attacks a person, organization, book, film, or idea in a way that is deliberately cruel, one-sided, and designed to destroy their reputation — not to inform or critique fairly.

Think of it this way: a fair critic asks, "What are the strengths and weaknesses here?" The person doing a hatchet job asks, "How do I make this person look as bad as possible?" Those are two completely different missions.
What Makes Something a "Hatchet Job"? (The Key Features)

A hatchet job has several defining features. Understanding each one will give you a complete picture:

1. The intent is to destroy, not to inform.
A hatchet job is not an honest critique that happens to be harsh. The purpose from the very beginning is to damage — someone's name, their career, their credibility, or their work. Everything in it is chosen to serve that goal.

2. It is deliberately one-sided.
A hatchet job ignores anything good or fair that could be said. If a politician has done ten things, nine of which are fine and one of which is questionable, a hatchet job will focus entirely on the questionable one and make it seem like the whole picture.

3. It uses facts unfairly.
A hatchet job often doesn't make things up completely — that would be easier to challenge. Instead, it cherry-picks real facts, quotes things out of context, exaggerates small flaws, and buries or ignores anything that contradicts its attack. The result looks factual but is deeply misleading.

4. It is typically done through a public platform.
Hatchet jobs usually appear in newspapers, magazines, TV broadcasts, online articles, or public speeches — anywhere an audience will see or hear them. The damage only works if people are watching.

5. There is often a personal or political motive behind it.
The person doing the hatchet job usually has something to gain — a rival politician wants to win an election, a competing business wants to weaken a competitor, a journalist has a personal grudge, or a powerful person wants to silence a critic.

These examples will show you how the term is used in real life:

  • A newspaper publishes a long article about a famous author. Instead of reviewing her new book fairly, the article digs up embarrassing personal stories from decades ago, twists her past statements, and frames everything to make her look dishonest. People who read it come away thinking she's terrible — even though the article left out all the good things about her. That's a hatchet job.
  • Two politicians are competing in an election. One of them releases a report filled with accusations, exaggerations, and misleading statistics about the other. The goal isn't to have a policy debate — it's to ruin the opponent's image before voters go to the polls. That's a hatchet job.
  • A film critic has a well-known personal dislike of a certain director. When the director releases a new movie, the critic writes a review that mocks every tiny detail, ignores what works, and makes the film sound catastrophically bad — even though most other reviewers thought it was decent. That's a hatchet job.
The Crucial Difference: Hatchet Job vs. Legitimate Harsh Criticism

This is an important distinction to understand, because a hatchet job can look like serious criticism on the surface.

Legitimate harsh criticism is honest and complete. A critic might say a book is poorly written, badly structured, and unconvincing — and give specific, fair reasons. It might be brutal, but it comes from an honest assessment. The critic would change their view if the evidence was different.

A hatchet job starts with the conclusion — "I want to damage this person" — and then works backwards to build a case. The evidence is selected, spun, or distorted to serve that pre-decided goal. No matter what the facts were, the attack was coming anyway.

The key question is: Was this written to honestly evaluate, or to deliberately destroy? If the answer is the latter, it's a hatchet job.
Common Ways the Phrase Is Used

You'll often hear or read it in these patterns:

  • "The magazine did a hatchet job on the CEO."
  • "That article was a complete hatchet job."
  • "He accused the reporter of doing a hatchet job on him."
  • "The documentary was nothing but a hatchet job dressed up as journalism."

The phrase is informal and slightly colourful. It's used in everyday conversation, journalism, and commentary — not in formal academic writing. When someone calls something a hatchet job, they are saying: this is an attack disguised as legitimate coverage.

The word "hatchet" (a small axe used for chopping) gives the phrase its energy. It suggests something violent and abrupt — not a careful, surgical critique, but a brutal, swinging blow meant to chop something down. That image captures the spirit of the phrase perfectly: a hatchet job doesn't chip away carefully at someone's reputation — it goes straight for the neck.

A hatchet job is a deliberately vicious, one-sided, and unfair public attack — usually in writing or broadcasting — designed not to inform or critique honestly, but to damage someone's or something's reputation as badly as possible.
7528:
A hatchling is a very young animal that has just come out of an egg — or one that came out of an egg very recently and is still in the earliest stage of its life.

The key idea locked inside this word is the egg. A hatchling is always an animal that was born by hatching — that is, by breaking open a shell from inside. This is what makes the word specific and precise. Not every young animal is a hatchling; only those that emerge from eggs qualify.

Any egg-laying animal can produce hatchlings. The word is used across a wide range of species:

  • Birds — a newly hatched sparrow, eagle, or penguin is a hatchling.
  • Reptiles — baby turtles, crocodiles, snakes, and lizards are all hatchlings when they first emerge from their eggs.
  • Fish — many fish lay eggs, and the tiny fish that emerge are hatchlings.
  • Insects — a young praying mantis or grasshopper that has just broken out of its egg can be called a hatchling.
  • Amphibians — frogs and toads hatch from eggs too, so the word applies here as well (though you'll often hear "tadpole" specifically for baby frogs, since they look so different from adults).
  • Dinosaurs (in palaeontology and fiction) — fossil evidence of dinosaur eggs exists, and young dinosaurs that had just emerged are called hatchlings.

The word is not used for mammals like dogs, cats, humans, or horses, because mammals give birth to live young — their babies don't hatch from eggs. For those, you use words like newborn, pup, cub, or kitten.
What Does a Hatchling Look, Act, and Feel Like?

Hatchlings are almost always:

  • Extremely small and fragile. They've just entered the world, so they are tiny, delicate, and vulnerable.
  • Not fully developed. Many hatchlings lack features the adult has. Baby birds, for example, are often bald, blind, and helpless when they first hatch. Their eyes may be sealed shut, and they have no feathers yet.
  • Dependent or independent, depending on the species. This is where hatchlings differ greatly from one another. A newly hatched baby robin is completely helpless and needs its parents to feed and warm it. A newly hatched sea turtle, on the other hand, is immediately independent — it scrambles out of the sand, heads straight for the ocean, and has to survive entirely on its own from the very first moment.
How Long Is an Animal Called a Hatchling?

The word "hatchling" refers specifically to the very early period just after hatching. It is a snapshot in time — the beginning of life outside the egg.

As the animal grows, it moves into the next stage and gets a different label. For example:

  • A bird hatchling grows into a nestling (still in the nest, growing feathers), then a fledgling (old enough to start learning to fly), and eventually a juvenile, and then an adult.
  • A reptile hatchling simply grows into a juvenile and then an adult.

So "hatchling" is not a permanent label — it describes only the earliest window of life.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Since you may encounter related words, here's how "hatchling" sits among them:

  • Newborn — a general word for any animal (or human) right after birth. It's broad and not specific to eggs. You can technically call a hatchling a newborn, but "hatchling" is more precise because it tells you the animal came from an egg.
  • Chick — specifically a baby bird. "Chick" is more informal and common in everyday speech; "hatchling" is more precise and is used in scientific or nature-writing contexts. A newly hatched bird can be called both.
  • Larva — the young stage of insects like butterflies or beetles, which looks completely different from the adult (think caterpillar vs. butterfly). Some insects hatch as larvae, so a larva could technically be called a hatchling, but "larva" is the more specific and standard term in those cases.
  • Fry — specifically the baby stage of fish, soon after hatching. Used in fish biology. "Hatchling" and "fry" can overlap for fish, but "fry" is the traditional fish-specific term.
  • Fledgling — an older, more developed young bird that is growing its flight feathers and learning to fly. This comes after the hatchling stage.

These will show you exactly how the word is used in real contexts:

  1. "The sea turtle hatchlings erupted from the sand in the middle of the night and raced toward the ocean."
  2. "The nest held three tiny hatchlings, their mouths open wide, waiting for their mother to bring food."
  3. "Scientists discovered a well-preserved fossil of a dinosaur hatchling near the nest site."
  4. "The snake hatchling was no longer than a pencil when it first slithered out of its leathery egg."
  5. "Wildlife volunteers carefully transported the crocodile hatchlings to a safer part of the river."

If you had to capture the entire meaning in one sentence:

A hatchling is a very young animal — one that has just hatched from an egg and is in the earliest, most fragile stage of its life outside the shell.

Everything else — the specific animal, how developed it is, how long it stays a hatchling — varies by species, but that core meaning stays constant.
7529:
"Hats off to someone" means you deeply admire, respect, or praise a person for something impressive, difficult, or admirable they have done.

When you say "hats off to someone," you are essentially saying:

"I think what you did is truly remarkable, and you deserve recognition for it."

It is an expression of genuine appreciation and honour. It is always positive. You use it when someone has done something that earns your respect — whether it's a big achievement, an act of bravery, hard work, kindness, or skill.
Where Does It Come From? (The Origin)

To understand an idiom well, you need to understand why those specific words were chosen. Here, the key word is "hat."

For centuries, across many cultures — especially in Europe — removing your hat in front of someone was one of the greatest gestures of respect you could offer. Think of it like a bow or a salute. Here is the history behind it:

  • Soldiers and knights would remove their helmets in front of royalty or a commanding officer to show they were not a threat and that they submitted respectfully.
  • Common people would take off their hats when a king, queen, or nobleman passed by as a sign of honour and loyalty.
  • Gentlemen in the 18th and 19th centuries would tip or fully remove their hats when greeting a lady or an important person as a mark of courtesy and admiration.
  • In churches and sacred places, men removed their hats to show reverence.

So, taking off your hat was essentially saying: "I lower myself before you. I honour you. You are worthy of my deepest respect."

Over time, even as the actual physical habit of wearing and tipping hats faded in daily life, the expression stayed alive in the English language as a way of saying "I give you the utmost respect."

The most common structure is:

"Hats off to [person/group] for [reason]!"

Let's look at examples across different situations so you can see how flexible this idiom is:

1. Praising hard work:

"Hats off to the entire team for finishing the project two days ahead of schedule!"

2. Admiring bravery:

"Hats off to the firefighters who risked their lives to save that family from the burning building."

3. Acknowledging a personal achievement:

"You raised three kids while working full time and still got your degree? Hats off to you!"

4. Recognising skill or talent:

"Hats off to the chef — that was honestly the best meal I've had in years."

5. Appreciating kindness:

"She donated her entire bonus to charity. Hats off to her for that kind gesture."

6. Admiring resilience:

"He rebuilt his life after losing everything. I have to say, hats off to him."

Notice that in every example, the person being praised has done something genuinely worthy of respect. This idiom is never used lightly or casually — it carries real weight and sincerity.
A Close Variation: "I Take My Hat Off to Someone"

You will also frequently hear the idiom in this form:

"I take my hat off to her — she handled that crisis brilliantly."

This means exactly the same thing. It is just a slightly longer, more personal way of saying it. Both versions are equally correct and widely used. Think of them as two sides of the same coin:

  • "Hats off to someone" — slightly more general, often used to praise a group or to make a statement.
  • "I take my hat off to someone" — slightly more personal, as if you yourself are performing the gesture of respect.

This idiom is:

  • ✅ Always positive — You can never use it to insult or mock someone.
  • ✅ Sincere — It carries genuine admiration, not empty flattery.
  • ✅ Suitable for all settings — You can use it in casual conversation with friends, in a speech, in writing, or even in a professional email.
  • ✅ Emotionally warm — It makes the person receiving the praise feel truly seen and valued.

Technically, like almost any phrase, it can be twisted into sarcasm with the right tone of voice, but this is rare and generally considered poor usage. In writing especially, "hats off to someone" is almost universally understood as genuine praise. If someone uses it sarcastically, it is usually very obvious from the context.

As a learner, you should treat it as a purely positive expression and use it only when you genuinely mean it.

It is important to clarify what this idiom does not mean:

  • ❌ It does not mean you literally want someone to remove a hat.
  • ❌ It is not a command or instruction.
  • ❌ It does not express agreement with an opinion — it praises an action or quality.

If you ever forget what this idiom means, just picture this scene in your mind:

A dignified gentleman in the old days, standing straight, slowly removing his hat and holding it to his chest as a great hero walks by.

That image — of deep, heartfelt respect being shown through the humble act of removing a hat — is the soul of this idiom. Every time you say "hats off to someone," you are performing that same gesture, just with words.
"Hats off to someone" = "I deeply respect and admire this person for what they have done."
